name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
title: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
answer: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of mapping the plausible readings of a statute, then building and testing arguments for and against each reading before an opponent does. In AI law it covers federal, state, and local rules that touch automated decision systems, data use, model training, and disclosure, along with older statutes that courts now apply to new technical facts. The scope includes definitions, exemptions, preemption questions, agency guidance, and the legislative history that surrounds each provision. With 6,940 state AI bills tracked on this site, the same phrase can carry different meanings across jurisdictions, which makes competing readings common rather than exceptional.

sections.body: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of mapping the plausible readings of a statute, then building and testing arguments for and against each reading before an opponent does. The scope includes definitions, exemptions, preemption questions, agency guidance, and the legislative history that surrounds each provision. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on primary sources first: bill texts, session laws, codes, regulations, committee reports, and court opinions, all kept in versioned form so amendments and effective dates are visible. Commercial legal research platforms, public legislative websites, and docket alert services supply search, citators, and tracking. AI-assisted tools can summarize, cluster, and compare large sets of provisions, but they sit on top of the source corpus and need citation checks against the original text. A working file often includes a comparison table, a definitions map, and a set of annotated excerpts that show where each reading gains or loses support.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts by isolating the operative language and the defined terms, then listing every ambiguity that could change the outcome. Practitioners apply the standard canons of construction, compare parallel provisions in related statutes, and review legislative history for signals about purpose and scope. They then write competing interpretations, red-team the strongest version of the opponent's reading, and test each against hypothetical facts that resemble the client's matter. AI can speed up the search and drafting, but the final product depends on human review of the exact words, the amendment record, and the controlling precedent.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on candor to the tribunal, protection of client confidences, and the provenance of every citation. Statutory text itself is generally public, but annotations, headnotes, and proprietary databases may carry license terms, so source tracking matters. The main risks are misquoting a provision, missing a later amendment, relying on an AI summary that drops a key exception, and exposing strategy through unsecured research files. Good practice keeps an audit trail from claim to source, separates public material from privileged work product, and treats any AI output as a draft that must be verified against the official text.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon points toward more statutes, more competing readings, and more court decisions that settle some ambiguities while opening others. As the site's 147 active AI lawsuits move through the system, adversarial statutory interpretation will appear in motions, briefs, and opinions about liability, disclosure, and preemption. Courts may develop canons or frameworks specific to AI, and legislatures may respond with clearer definitions or targeted amendments. The research practice will likely become more continuous, with teams monitoring bill changes and case law in parallel rather than treating interpretation as a one-time memo.
